```{r}
#| label: original-study
#| include: false
# The original study's numbers, entered once and used by the power analysis, the Key
# statistics table, and the side-by-side figures. Replace these with your original study's
# values, and say in a comment exactly where in the paper each one comes from.
#
# Schapiro et al. (2013), Experiment 2. N = 10: "experiment 2 had ten participants" (Online
# Methods, Participants). Key test: participants "pressed the spacebar on passing into a new
# cluster significantly more often than at other times in the sequence (t9 = 2.30, P < 0.05;
# Fig. 2b)".
# This is a paired t-test (transition vs. other parse probability, within participants). The
# paper gives only the t values and "P < 0.05", not the means or SDs, so the effect size is
# derived from t: Cohen's d_z = t / sqrt(N), with p and the 95% CI on d_z recomputed from t.
# Fig. 2b plots the means (±1 SEM) but they are not stated in the text.

# 95% CI on d_z from a paired t, by inverting the noncentral t distribution.
dz_ci <- function(t, n, level = 0.95) {
  df <- n - 1
  ncp_at <- function(q) uniroot(function(ncp) pt(t, df, ncp) - q, c(-40, 40))$root
  c(ncp_at((1 + level) / 2), ncp_at((1 - level) / 2)) / sqrt(n)
}
original <- tibble(
  paths = c("All trials", "Hamiltonian paths"),
  N     = 10,
  t     = c(2.30, 2.35)
) |>
  mutate(df = N - 1,
         p  = 2 * pt(-abs(t), df),
         estimate = t / sqrt(N),
         ci_low  = map2_dbl(t, N, ~ dz_ci(.x, .y)[1]),
         ci_high = map2_dbl(t, N, ~ dz_ci(.x, .y)[2]))
# The key test is the one on all trials.
original_key <- original |> filter(paths == "All trials")
original_dz  <- original_key$estimate
```

# Key statistics

```{r}
#| label: analysis-functions
#| code-summary: "Show the analysis code (shared by Phase 1 and Phase 2)"

# Load one phase's exported data and apply the exclusion rule. Returns NULL if that phase
# has not been exported yet, which is how every section below knows to skip itself.
read_phase <- function(id) {
  dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw", id)
  if (!all(file.exists(file.path(dir, c("participants.csv", "trials.csv"))))) return(NULL)
  participants <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "participants.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  trials       <- read_csv(file.path(dir, "trials.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
  errors_path  <- file.path(dir, "errors.csv")
  errors <- if (file.exists(errors_path)) read_csv(errors_path, show_col_types = FALSE) else tibble()

  complete <- participants |> filter(completed)

  # Exclusion rule (Analysis plan): exclude participants who did not complete the study, who
  # were correct on less than 50% of exposure-phase rotation judgments, who responded to less
  # than 70% of exposure-phase images, or who took more than 90 minutes in total.
  exposure <- trials |>
    filter(task == "exposure") |>
    group_by(participant_id) |>
    summarise(exp_acc           = mean(as.logical(correct), na.rm = TRUE),
              exp_response_rate = mean(!as.logical(timed_out), na.rm = TRUE),
              .groups = "drop")
  checked <- complete |>
    left_join(exposure, by = "participant_id") |>
    mutate(duration_min = as.numeric(difftime(lubridate::as_datetime(ended_at),
                                              lubridate::as_datetime(started_at), units = "mins")))
  keep <- checked |>
    filter(!is.na(exp_acc), exp_acc >= 0.50, exp_response_rate >= 0.70,
           !is.na(duration_min), duration_min <= 90)

  list(participants = participants, trials = trials, errors = errors,
       complete = complete, keep = keep,
       # Sessions with no response to any exposure image (what a device without a keyboard produces).
       n_no_response = sum(checked$exp_response_rate %in% 0))
}

# Parse probabilities for Fig. 2b: for each analysed participant, the proportion of
# opportunities on which they pressed the spacebar at a community transition and elsewhere,
# for all parsing trials and for Hamiltonian-path trials only. A community transition is
# arrival in a new community after at least four consecutive steps in another (Online
# Methods). "Other" is images that are not a transition at all; transitions after a shorter
# run (1-3 steps) are left out of both.
parse_probs <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "parsing", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    mutate(parsed = as.logical(parsed), community_change = as.logical(community_change),
           type = case_when(community_change & prev_run >= 4 ~ "Community transition parse",
                            !community_change               ~ "Other parse")) |>
    filter(!is.na(type)) |>
    (\(x) bind_rows(mutate(x, paths = "All trials"),
                    filter(x, walk_type == "hamiltonian") |> mutate(paths = "Hamiltonian paths")))() |>
    group_by(participant_id, paths, type) |>
    summarise(p = mean(parsed), n_opportunities = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(type = factor(type, levels = c("Community transition parse", "Other parse")))
}

# Paired t-test of transition vs. other parse probability, in the columns of `original`.
parse_test <- function(probs) {
  w <- probs |>
    select(participant_id, paths, type, p) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = p) |>
    drop_na()
  w |>
    group_by(paths) |>
    filter(n() >= 2) |>
    summarise({
      tt <- t.test(`Community transition parse`, `Other parse`, paired = TRUE)
      n <- n()
      tibble(N = n, df = unname(tt$parameter), t = unname(tt$statistic), p = tt$p.value,
             estimate = unname(tt$statistic) / sqrt(n),
             ci_low = dz_ci(unname(tt$statistic), n)[1], ci_high = dz_ci(unname(tt$statistic), n)[2])
    }, .groups = "drop")
}

# The key test for one phase: the paired t on all parsing trials, or NULL until there are at
# least two analysed participants.
key_test <- function(d) {
  r <- parse_test(parse_probs(d)) |> filter(paths == "All trials")
  if (nrow(r) == 0) NULL else r
}

# Bar plot analogous to Fig. 2b: mean parse probability by type, all trials and Hamiltonian
# paths, error bars ±1 SEM across participants, * where the paired t-test gives p < .05.
parse_plot <- function(probs) {
  means <- probs |>
    group_by(paths, type) |>
    summarise(mean = mean(p), sem = sd(p) / sqrt(n()), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
  tests <- parse_test(probs) |>
    left_join(means |> group_by(paths) |> summarise(top = max(mean + coalesce(sem, 0))), by = "paths") |>
    mutate(label = if_else(p < 0.05, "*", "n.s."))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(means, aes(x = paths, y = mean, fill = type)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75, colour = "black") +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sem, ymax = mean + sem), position = dodge, width = 0.2) +
    geom_text(data = tests, aes(x = paths, y = top + 0.02, label = label), inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 5) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Community transition parse" = "grey25", "Other parse" = "grey85")) +
    scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Probability of parse", fill = NULL) +
    theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

# The key comparison's raw counts: how many analysed participants chose the risky program
# in each frame.
risky_counts <- function(d) {
  d$trials |>
    filter(task == "framing", participant_id %in% d$keep$participant_id) |>
    group_by(condition) |>
    summarise(risky = sum(choice == "risky"), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
}

# The key statistic: difference in the proportion choosing the risky program (loss minus
# gain) with a 95% CI, and the uncorrected chi-square, which is the same test. NULL until
# both frames have at least one analysed participant.
diff_ci <- function(counts) {
  loss <- counts[counts$condition == "loss", ]
  gain <- counts[counts$condition == "gain", ]
  if (nrow(loss) == 0 || nrow(gain) == 0) return(NULL)
  pt <- prop.test(c(loss$risky, gain$risky), c(loss$n, gain$n), correct = FALSE)
  tibble(N = loss$n + gain$n,
         estimate = unname(pt$estimate[1] - pt$estimate[2]),
         ci_low = pt$conf.int[1], ci_high = pt$conf.int[2],
         statistic = unname(pt$statistic), p = pt$p.value)
}

# Side-by-side figure: any number of studies on the same axes, in the order given.
prop_ci <- function(x, n) {
  ci <- prop.test(x, n, correct = FALSE)$conf.int
  tibble(p = x / n, low = ci[1], high = ci[2])
}
comparison_plot <- function(...) {
  studies <- list(...)
  studies <- studies[!map_lgl(studies, ~ is.null(.x) || nrow(.x) == 0)]
  df <- imap_dfr(studies, ~ mutate(.x, Study = .y)) |>
    rowwise() |> mutate(prop_ci(risky, n)) |> ungroup() |>
    mutate(Study = factor(Study, levels = names(studies)), label = sprintf("n = %d", n))
  fills <- setNames(c("grey55", "#1E6E76", "#B8792A")[seq_along(studies)], names(studies))
  dodge <- position_dodge(width = 0.8)
  ggplot(df, aes(x = condition, y = p, fill = Study)) +
    geom_col(position = dodge, width = 0.75) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), position = dodge, width = 0.2) +
    geom_text(aes(y = 0.02, label = label), position = dodge, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "white") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = fills) +
    labs(x = "Frame", y = "Chose the risky program", fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(legend.position = "top")
}

phase1 <- read_phase(experiment_id)
phase2 <- read_phase(experiment_id_phase2)
have_data   <- !is.null(phase1)
have_phase2 <- !is.null(phase2)
```

```{r}
#| label: key-stats
#| echo: false
# Each row needs N, df, t, p, and d_z as estimate / ci_low / ci_high (the columns of `original`).
# Phase 2 still uses the Phase 1 test until its design is settled.
fmt_row <- function(study, r) {
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(Study = study, N = "", `Effect (d_z)` = "not yet collected",
                  `95% CI` = "", t = "", p = ""))
  }
  tibble(Study = study, N = as.character(r$N),
         `Effect (d_z)` = sprintf("%.2f", r$estimate),
         `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", r$ci_low, r$ci_high),
         t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", r$df, r$t),
         p = format.pval(r$p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001))
}
bind_rows(
  fmt_row("Original (Exp. 2)", original_key),
  fmt_row("Phase 1: replication", if (have_data) key_test(phase1)),
  fmt_row("Phase 2: extension", if (have_phase2) key_test(phase2))
) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrllll",
               caption = "Key comparison: parse probability at community transitions vs. elsewhere in the sequence, all trials, paired t-test. Original values are from Schapiro et al. (2013), Experiment 2; its d_z, 95% CI and exact p are recomputed from the reported t9 = 2.30 (reported as P < 0.05).")
```

# Phase 1: Replication

## Introduction

### Connection to My Research Interest

I am interested in how the hippocampus processes temporally sequential input when there is no supervision. If there are underlying statistical relationships between the stimuli, can the hippocampus detect and encode these? Furthermore, when a new sequence of stimuli that shares some of these regularities is presented later, can the hippocampus learn it faster than when it learned the previous one, taking advantage of what it already knows? Finally, if the hippocampus is capable of extracting and learning such regularities, what is the synapse-level learning mechanism that enables it? Schapiro et al. (2013) provides the foundation for exploring this, presenting evidence that humans can extract temporal regularity from sequentially-presented, random-looking images. Even though this paper doesn't specifically focus on the hippocampus, it shows the exact human cognitive capability I am interested in, and furthermore, its task closely resembles the one I am devising to train my hippocampus-inspired artificial neural network. As the final goal of my own research project is to propose a prediction about human behavior drawn from my artificial hippocampus and see if that prediction holds in human subjects, running this "mock-experiment" here will be greatly helpful.

### Stimuli and Procedure

#### Stimuli

15 distinct visual stimuli were created in ArtMatic Pro (http://www.artmatic.com/), and randomly assigned to the nodes of the graph for each participant. The graph had three communities of five nodes each, every node had four neighbors, and all transitions were equally probable. For the sequence exposure phase, a sequence of total 1,400 images (with duplicated images) was generated by a random walk on the graph, with about 20% of images rotated 90°. For the parsing phase, a sequence of 600 images alternated between blocks of 15 items that were generated from a random walk and blocks of 15 items from a Hamiltonian path (a path visiting each node exactly once).

#### Procedure

The experiment begun with the sequence exposure phase. The participants first saw all the stimuli on the screen. Then, each stimulus in the sequence was shown one at a time for 1.5 s without any interstimulus interval. Participants pressed one key when they think the stimulus was rotated and another key otherwise, responding on every trial. A beep at one frequency was played when the response was incorrect and at another frequency when the response was not given during the stimulus presentation. In the parsing phase, similarly, the participants saw each stimulus one at a time for 1.5 s. During the images were presented, the participants pressed the spacebar when they thought there should be a breaking point, therefore segmenting the sequence in a way that they felt was natural. A possible challenge I foresee is that, since the duration of the task is long, keeping participants attentive throughout the session could be hard.

### Key Statistical Test

For both random-walk-generated paths and Hamiltonian paths, the participants were expected to parse the sequence at community cluster transitions (beginning in a new community after at least four consecutive steps in another) significantly more often than at other times in the sequence. This comparison was tested using two-tailed paired-samples t-test, since the same group of participants contributed to both quantities.

### Possible Extension

A hypothesis I can test without running an additional experiment is: can visual similarity of the images account for the parsing effect? To test this, I would compute the cosine similarity between pixel values of consecutive images and see whether the participants tend to place fewer boundaries between highly similar images than the ones with less similarity.

## Methods

### Power analysis

```{r}
#| label: power
# Paired t-test: with sd = 1, delta is d_z and n is the number of participants.
power_rows <- map_dfr(c(0.80, 0.90, 0.95), function(pw) {
  n <- power.t.test(delta = original_dz, sd = 1, power = pw, sig.level = 0.05,
                    type = "paired")$n
  tibble(power = scales::percent(pw), n_total = ceiling(n))
})

original_effect <- original_dz
two_and_half <- ceiling(2.5 * original_key$N)

knitr::kable(power_rows, col.names = c("Power", "N participants"),
             caption = sprintf(
               "Sample needed to detect the original effect (Experiment 2, d_z = %.2f, from t9 = %.2f with N = %d), paired t-test, two-sided alpha = .05.",
               original_dz, original_key$t, original_key$N))
```

For comparison, 2.5 times the original sample (N=10) would be N=`r two_and_half`. I decided to use the sample size that provides 80% power (N=17), since it requires fewer participants than the 2.5 times original sample size, and I have a limited budget for recruiting participants.

### Planned sample

The experiment will be implemented online, and participants will be recruited on Prolific from US residents who are fluent in English and 18 or older. I plan to recruit 17 valid samples that pass the exclusion criteria. I will exclude participants who did not complete the study, who scored less than 50% or responded less than 70% in the exposure phase which reflects task compliance, and who took more than one hour and a half. The reason for the last exclusion criterion is that the study, without any breaks, takes slightly more than 50 minutes in total. Participants can take breaks between phases (e.g., when they switch from the exposure phase to the parsing phase), but if they take breaks that are too long, their memory for the stimuli may decay, and the results may not be reflecting the effect that I aim to observe.
  
### Materials

The experiment requires 15 distinct visual stimuli with circular boundaries that are radial. These stimuli should not look identical when rotated by 90°. The authors of the original study did not provide the stimuli they used; they indicated the software they used to generate the stimuli (ArtMatic Pro), but I did not have access to the software. Therefore, I created my own stimuli following the described criteria. The code to generate the stimuli is included in the repository at `/scripts/make-stimuli.js`, and the generated stimuli are included in `/stimuli`.

### Procedure

#### Welcome and demographics
Once participants access the website, they must agree to the consent form presented on the first page. After a welcoming message, they are instructed to turn on audio, as they will receive audio feedback during the experiment. Then, they are prompted to provide demographics including age, gender, and first language.

#### Exposure phase (35 minutes + 4 short breaks)
The exposure phase begins with participants viewing 50 abstract images with circular boundaries. The instructions specify that these images are in their normal orientation, but in the following experiment, participants will be asked whether each image is rotated from its normal orientation. Participants can take as much time as needed to familiarize themselves with the images. On the next page, more detailed instructions—including the keys to press to indicate rotation—are provided. The instructions also clarify that participants will receive audio feedback for incorrect responses or failure to respond during stimulus presentation.

Then, the test phase begins. Participants view a sequence of 1,400 images, one at a time, for 1.5 seconds each. They press key J if they think the image is rotated and key F if they think it is in its original orientation. A low-frequency beep plays for incorrect responses and a higher-frequency beep for missed responses during the 1.5-second stimulus presentation window. Every 7 minutes, participants can choose to take a short break.

#### Parsing phase (15 minute)
After the test phase, instructions for the parsing phase are provided. Participants are told they will view a sequence of images similar to the test phase and press the spacebar when they think there should be a breaking point. When ready, the parsing phase begins (15 minutes). A sequence of 600 images, all in their normal orientation, is shown one at a time for 1.5 seconds each. Participants can decide whether to place a breakpoint anytime during sequence presentation.

#### Feedback and debriefing
Once participants complete the parsing phase, a brief feedback page appears. Participants are asked to provide optional responses about whether the instructions were clear and any comments about the study. Finally, a debriefing page explaining the study’s goal, what we aim to measure, and contact information (suheecho@stanford.edu) is shown.

### Analysis plan

**Key analysis of interest.** For both random walk-generated part of the sequence and Hamiltonian path-generated part of the sequence, the proportion of break points placed at community transitions is higher than the proportion of break points placed somewhere else, tested with a two-tailed paired-samples t-test. The effect size is Cohen's d_z computed as (p_{community transition} - p_{other}), with a 95% confidence interval.

**Exclusions.** Participants are excluded if they did not complete the study, scored less than 50% in the exposure phase, responded to less than 70% of the stimuli in the exposure phase,or they took more than one hour and half to complete the entire study.

### Differences from the original study

| Aspect | Original study | This replication | Expected to matter? |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Sample | Members of the Princeton community paid $12/h or given course credit. | Adults recruited on Prolific. | Not likely. |
| Setting | Offline in the lab. | Online, unsupervised, on the participant's own computer. | Possibly, since the study is about an hour long. The participants' attention may be lower online. |
| Procedure | The participants took a short break every 7 minutes during the exposure phase. | I followed the original study's procedure, but did not control the break duration. | Likely. I assume that the breaks in the original study were shorter and within the lab. That said, it is hard to control the participants' breaks when they are participating online. If the breaks are too long and if the participants engage in other activities during the breaks, it might affect their performance. |
| Materials | 15 ArtMatic Pro-generated abstract fractal images (Fig. 1c of the original paper). | Generated grayscale circular images with radial symmetry. | Not likely. |
| Response | During the exposure phase, the participants were asked to press two different keys to respond, and the keys were not specified in the paper. | I used keys F and J. | Not likely. |
| Analyses | The paper does not report any exclusion rule. | I introduced some exclusion criteria described in the section above, mainly in order to ensure data quality because I am recruiting participants and running the experiment online. | Not likely. |

```{r}
  filter(task == "demographics", participant_id %in% keep$participant_id) |>
  mutate(resp = map(response, ~ fromJSON(.x))) |>
  transmute(
    participant_id,
    age    = map_dbl(resp, ~ as.numeric(.x$age %||% NA)),
    gender = map_chr(resp, ~ as.character(.x$gender %||% NA))
  )

if (nrow(demo) > 0) {
  demo |>
    summarise(N = n(), `Mean age` = round(mean(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `SD age` = round(sd(age, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
              `Age not given` = sum(is.na(age))) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Age of the analysed sample.")
}
```

## Results

### Data preparation

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Data preparation follows the analysis plan. Loading and exclusions are done by the shared analysis code under Key statistics (open "Show the analysis code"). Describe anything you did to the data beyond that.

### Confirmatory analysis

```{r}
#| label: confirmatory
#| eval: !expr have_data
# Two-tailed paired t-test of parse probability at community transitions vs. other images,
# for all parsing trials (the key test) and for Hamiltonian paths only.
probs <- parse_probs(phase1)
tests <- parse_test(probs)

if (nrow(tests) == 0) {
  message("Paired t-test not run: it needs at least two analysed participants; there are ",
          n_distinct(probs$participant_id), ".")
}
if (nrow(tests) > 0) {
  probs |>
    group_by(Trials = paths, type) |>
    summarise(`Mean parse probability` = round(mean(p), 3), SD = round(sd(p), 3), N = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Parse probability by opportunity type, mean and SD across analysed participants.")
}
if (nrow(tests) > 0) {
  tests |>
    transmute(Trials = paths, N, t = sprintf("t(%d) = %.2f", df, t),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001),
              `d_z [95% CI]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", estimate, ci_low, ci_high)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Paired t-tests, community transition vs. other parse probability.")
}
```

### Replication assessment

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Judge the replication on effect sizes, not only on whether the key test is significant. Compare the replication estimate and its interval with the original: does the interval exclude zero, and does it include the original estimate? A significant result much smaller than the original, or a non-significant result whose interval still includes the original effect, are both informative and should be reported as such (Experimentology §3.2).
:::

```{r}
#| label: comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
orig <- original_key
rep  <- key_test(phase1)

if (!is.null(rep)) {
  bind_rows(orig |> mutate(Study = "Original (Exp. 2)"), rep |> mutate(Study = "Phase 1: replication")) |>
    transmute(Study, N,
              `Effect (d_z)` = sprintf("%.2f", estimate),
              `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", ci_low, ci_high),
              p = format.pval(p, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)) |>
    knitr::kable(caption = "Effect size: Cohen's d_z for community transition vs. other parse probability, all trials. The original's d_z and CI are recomputed from its reported t9 = 2.30.")
} else {
  message("Replication effect size not computed yet: need at least two analysed participants.")
}
```

```{r}
#| label: comparison-verdict
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (!is.null(rep)) {
  excludes_zero <- rep$ci_low > 0 | rep$ci_high < 0
  includes_orig <- orig$estimate >= rep$ci_low & orig$estimate <= rep$ci_high
  cat(sprintf(
    "The replication's 95%% interval %s zero and %s the original estimate of d_z = %.2f. ",
    if (excludes_zero) "excludes" else "includes",
    if (includes_orig) "includes" else "does not include",
    orig$estimate))
  cat("These two facts are the starting point for the summary in the Discussion, not the conclusion.\n")
}
```

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: show the original next to your replication

**Every report should have a figure that puts the original finding and your replication side by side.** It is the single most informative thing in a replication report: a reader can see at a glance whether the effect came back, and how its size compares. Make it however you can, in roughly this order of preference:

1.  **Replot both from numbers.** Enter the original's summary statistics (means or proportions, with SDs, SEs or CIs, and Ns) in the original-study chunk at the top of this file, and plot them on the same axes as yours. That is what the demo figure below does.

2.  **Replot the original from its data**, if the authors shared it or it is in an open repository, using exactly the same plotting code as for your own data.

3.  **Show the original figure as an image** next to yours if neither is possible. Save a screenshot of it, for example as `writeup/images/original-figure.png`, and lay the two out in columns:

    ```` markdown
    ::: {layout-ncol=2}
    ![Original: Tversky & Kahneman (1981), Figure 1](images/original-figure.png)

    ```{{r}}
    # your replication plot here
    ```
    :::
    ````

Whichever you choose, use the same measure, scale, condition order and error-bar meaning for both panels, label which is which, and cite the source of the original values or figure in the caption. If the original reported no variability, say so rather than leaving it out silently.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-comparison
#| eval: !expr have_data
#| fig-cap: "Phase 1 replication of Schapiro et al. (2013), Fig. 2b: proportion of opportunities on which analysed participants parsed at a community transition (arrival in a new community after at least four steps in another) and at non-transition images, for all parsing trials and for Hamiltonian paths only. Error bars are ±1 SEM across participants; * p < .05, paired t-test. The original reports these means only graphically (Fig. 2b, N = 10; t9 = 2.30 for all trials and t9 = 2.35 for Hamiltonian paths)."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4
probs <- parse_probs(phase1)
if (nrow(probs) > 0) parse_plot(probs) else message("No analysed participants yet, so there is nothing to plot.")
```

# Phase 2: Extension

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance: choosing your extension

Follow the Extension guidelines page on Canvas. In brief:

- **By default the extension is a best-practices modification of your Phase 1 experiment.** If your replication did not succeed, it is a **rescue**: address the plausible reasons for the failure. If it did succeed, it is an **upgrade**: make the estimate more precise. Typical changes are better or more reliable measurement, more trials, a within-participant design where that is legitimate, comprehension and manipulation checks, clearer instructions, or a larger or better-targeted sample.
- **If your scientific extension pitch was approved at Milestone 3 and your replication succeeded, propose that instead:** the original conditions rerun unchanged, plus the one added condition or manipulation, with a power analysis for the new comparison.
- On either track you may add exploratory measures **at the end** of the study.
- Every change is listed and tagged by category below; everything else stays identical.

State your track on the line below, and delete the others.
:::

**Track:** Best-practices upgrade / Best-practices rescue / Scientific extension (approved at Milestone 3)

## Rationale

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

One or two paragraphs. For a rescue: what are the plausible reasons Phase 1 did not reproduce the original result, and how does each change address one of them? For an upgrade: where is the Phase 1 estimate least precise or least trustworthy, and how will the changes improve it? For a scientific extension: what question does the added condition answer, and why does it follow from the original finding?
:::

## Changes from Phase 1

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Every change from the Phase 1 experiment, one per row, each tagged with a category: Measurement, Trials, Design, Checks, Instructions, Sample, Added condition (scientific track only), or Exploratory measure (end of study only). If it is not in this table, it does not change: same materials, wording, procedure, exclusion rule and analysis. The rows below are examples for the demo; replace them with yours.
:::

| \# | Category | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Why |
|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|---------------|
| 1 | Sample | 27 analysed participants | 300 analysed participants (150 per frame) | Phase 1's interval was too wide to distinguish the original effect from a much smaller one. |
| 2 | Checks | No comprehension check | After the choice, participants say how many people are at risk (600) | Confirms participants read the scenario; failures are reported, and excluded only if preregistered. |
| 3 | Exploratory measure | None | At the end: "How confident are you in your choice?" (1–7) | Exploratory only; collected after every confirmatory measure. |

Everything not listed above is identical to Phase 1.

## Power and sample

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Guidance

Justify the Phase 2 sample, and **state how you expect the estimate and its precision to compare with Phase 1**. For an upgrade, plan the sample around the confidence interval you want; for a rescue, around the power to detect the original effect, or the smallest effect you would still consider a successful replication; for a scientific extension, around the power to detect the new comparison. Set `phase2_n_per_group` in the code below; the table uses Phase 1's estimate if you have it and the original's otherwise.
:::

```{r}
#| label: phase2-power
# Within-subject design: every participant contributes both parse probabilities, so this is the
# number of analysed participants in Phase 2, not a per-condition count.
phase2_n_per_group <- 150

# Phase 1 estimate, in the same columns as `original` (N, df, t, p, estimate = d_z, ci_low, ci_high).
p1_stats <- if (have_data) key_test(phase1)
basis <- if (!is.null(p1_stats)) list(dz = p1_stats$estimate, source = "Phase 1") else
  list(dz = original_dz, source = "the original study")

# Expected 95% CI half-width on d_z at n participants (large-sample approximation).
half_width <- function(n, dz) qt(0.975, n - 1) * sqrt(1 / n + dz^2 / (2 * n))
power_at <- function(n, dz) {
  tryCatch(power.t.test(n = n, delta = dz, sd = 1, sig.level = 0.05, type = "paired")$power,
           error = function(e) NA)
}

rows <- tibble(
  Study = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) "Phase 1 (actual)", "Phase 2 (planned)"),
  `N analysed` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) p1_stats$N, phase2_n_per_group),
  `95% CI half-width` = c(if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("±%.2f", (p1_stats$ci_high - p1_stats$ci_low) / 2),
                          sprintf("±%.2f (expected)", half_width(phase2_n_per_group, basis$dz)))
)
knitr::kable(rows, caption = sprintf("Precision of the key estimate (d_z), Phase 2 expected values based on %s.", basis$source))

tibble(
  `Effect to detect` = c(sprintf("Original: d_z = %.2f", original_dz),
                         if (!is.null(p1_stats)) sprintf("Phase 1: d_z = %.2f", p1_stats$estimate),
                         sprintf("Half the original: d_z = %.2f", original_dz / 2)),
  `Power at planned N` = scales::percent(c(
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_dz),
    if (!is.null(p1_stats)) power_at(phase2_n_per_group, p1_stats$estimate),
    power_at(phase2_n_per_group, original_dz / 2)
  ), accuracy = 1)
) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = sprintf("Power of the Phase 2 key test (paired t) at %d participants, two-sided alpha = .05.", phase2_n_per_group))
```

```{r}
#| label: phase2-results

            nrow(phase2$participants), nrow(phase2$complete), nrow(phase2$keep)))
if (!is.null(p2_stats)) {

  cat(sprintf("Key comparison: %.0f points [%.0f, %.0f], chi-square(1) = %.2f, %s.\n",
              100 * p2_stats$estimate, 100 * p2_stats$ci_low, 100 * p2_stats$ci_high,
              p2_stats$statistic, p_text))
}
```
